lesson.intro: When a problem keeps asking "what is the smallest or largest item right now?" while items arrive, use a heap: O(1) peek, O(log n) push and pop. Learn how it works, Python's heapq, a short JavaScript heap, and the top-k and merge patterns.
objectives: Explain the heap property and the array index arithmetic
Trace sift up and sift down, and state their O(log n) cost
Use heapq with negation for max-heaps and tie-breaking tuples
Write a small comparator-based MinHeap in JavaScript
Solve top-k and k-way merge problems in O(n log k)

sections.title: The problem a heap solves
sections.key: A min-heap keeps every parent no larger than its children, so the minimum sits at the root: peek in O(1), push and pop in O(log n).
sections.body:
An emergency room treats the most urgent patient next while new patients keep arriving. You need two fast operations, again and again: add an item, and remove the most urgent one. That is a **priority queue**.

[[visual]]

A **min-heap** is a binary tree with one rule, the **heap property**: every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest value is the root. A **max-heap** flips the rule.

[[visual 2]]

The rule says nothing about left versus right or about cousins. A heap is only partially ordered: the second smallest could be either child of the root, and the array is usually not sorted. That loose rule is why a heap is cheaper to maintain than a sorted list.

Heaps power job schedulers and timers, Dijkstra's shortest paths, merging sorted files, top 10 lists and running medians.

visual.title: Ways to build a priority queue
visual.caption: A heap also peeks at the minimum in O(1).

visual.title: A min-heap
visual.caption: 3 is larger than its sibling 2, and that is fine: siblings and cousins are unordered.

sections.pitfall: Thinking a heap keeps everything sorted. It only guarantees the root. If you need all values in order, popping them one by one costs O(n log n), the same as sorting.

check.question: Which statement is true of every min-heap?
choices: The array holding the heap is sorted
Every left child is smaller than its right sibling
Each parent is less than or equal to its children
The largest value is always in the bottom level
check.explanation: The heap property only relates parents and children. Siblings are unordered, the array is usually not sorted, and the largest value is a leaf but not necessarily on the bottom level: a leaf can sit one level higher in a heap whose last level is not full.

sections.title: The array layout: a tree without pointers
sections.key: A heap is a complete binary tree stored level by level in an array, so index math finds relatives: the children of i sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
sections.body:
A heap is drawn as a tree but stored as a plain array. It is always a **complete binary tree**: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left with no gaps. So you can write it level by level into an array and compute where each node's relatives live.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The parent of i is at `(i - 1) // 2`, and a child index past the end means no such child.

The last element is always the last leaf, which push and pop rely on. A complete tree of n nodes has height `floor(log2 n)`, so any walk from the root to a leaf is O(log n).

Some textbooks use 1-based indexes (children `2i` and `2i + 1`, parent `i // 2`); `heapq` is 0-based. Never mix them.

visual.title: The same heap as an array
visual.caption: Index 1 (value 3) has children at 2 x 1 + 1 = 3 and 2 x 1 + 2 = 4: the values 7 and 4. The parent of index 5 is (5 - 1) // 2 = 2.

sections.code:
heap = [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]

def left(i):   return 2 * i + 1
def right(i):  return 2 * i + 2
def parent(i): return (i - 1) // 2

print(heap[left(1)], heap[right(1)])               # 7 4
print(heap[parent(5)])                             # 2
print(left(2) < len(heap), right(2) < len(heap))   # True False
sections.deeper: **Why arrays make heaps fast.** There are no node objects and no pointers to follow, and parents sit near their children in memory, so the processor's cache works well. Pointer-based trees pay for each hop.
sections.pitfall: Assuming `heap[1]` is the second smallest value. In `[1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]` the second smallest is 2, at index 2. Only `heap[0]` is guaranteed.

check.question: In a 0-based heap array, where is the parent of the node at index 8?
choices: Index 4
Index 3
Index 2
Index 7
check.explanation: (8 - 1) // 2 = 3. Index 4 is what the 1-based formula i // 2 would give, which is the classic mix-up. Check: the children of 3 are 7 and 8.

sections.title: Sift up and sift down
sections.key: Push appends at the end and sifts up past larger parents; pop moves the last leaf to the root and sifts down, always swapping with the smaller child.
sections.body:
**Push:** append the value at the end, the only spot that keeps the tree complete. Then **sift up**: while it is smaller than its parent, swap the two.

**Pop:** the minimum is at index 0. Move the last element into the root, shrink the array by one, then **sift down**: while it is larger than its smaller child, swap with that child. Only the smaller child can become a parent no larger than both children.

[[visual]]

Each move walks one root-to-leaf path, so push and pop are O(log n); peek is O(1).

Pushing n values one at a time costs O(n log n). **Heapify** sifts down every non-leaf node from the last back to the root: most nodes sit near the bottom and move a step or two, so it is O(n).

visual.title: Push 0, then pop the minimum

steps.label: 0 < parent 1 at index 0: swap
steps.note: 0 is the root: sift up stops

steps.label: Pop: save 0, move the last value 2 to the root
The smaller child is 1 at index 2: swap
steps.note: 2 is a leaf now: sift down stops

visual.result: Returned 0, and the heap is `[1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]` again

sections.code:
def push(heap, val):
    heap.append(val)
    i = len(heap) - 1
    while i > 0 and heap[i] < heap[(i - 1) // 2]:   # smaller than parent
        p = (i - 1) // 2
        heap[i], heap[p] = heap[p], heap[i]
        i = p

def pop(heap):
    top = heap[0]
    last = heap.pop()              # remove the last leaf
    if heap:
        heap[0] = last             # move it to the root
        i = 0
        while True:
            l, r = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
            smallest = i
            if l < len(heap) and heap[l] < heap[smallest]:
                smallest = l
            if r < len(heap) and heap[r] < heap[smallest]:
                smallest = r
            if smallest == i:
                break
            heap[i], heap[smallest] = heap[smallest], heap[i]
            i = smallest
    return top

h = [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]
push(h, 0)
print(h)        # [0, 3, 1, 7, 4, 5, 2]
print(pop(h))   # 0
print(h)        # [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]
sections.pitfall: Swapping with the left child by default during sift down. Always swap with the smaller child; otherwise the larger child becomes the parent of the smaller one and the heap property breaks.

check.question: You pop from the min-heap `[2, 5, 3, 8, 6, 4]`. The last value, 4, moves to the root. What is the array after sift down?
check.explanation: After removing the last element and placing 4 at the root you have [4, 5, 3, 8, 6]. The children of the root are 5 and 3; the smaller is 3, and 4 > 3, so they swap: [3, 5, 4, 8, 6]. Index 2 has no children (5 and 6 are past the end), so sifting stops.

sections.title: Python's heapq: a min-heap on a plain list
sections.key: Python's `heapq` treats a plain list as a min-heap: negate values for a max-heap, and push `(priority, count, item)` so ties never compare the items.
sections.body:
Python has no heap class. The `heapq` functions treat an ordinary list as a min-heap:

[[visual]]

**Max-heap:** push `-x` and negate again when you pop. The largest value becomes the most negative, so it sits at the root.

**Priorities with data:** push tuples like `(priority, item)`. Tuples compare element by element, so on a tie Python compares the items, which raises `TypeError` for dicts. Put a counter in the middle, `(priority, count, item)`; equal priorities then leave in insertion order.

Every function assumes the list already is a heap. Call `heappop` on a hand-built list without `heapify` and you get wrong answers, not an error.

visual.title: The heapq functions
rows: Remove and return the smallest: O(log n)
Peek at the smallest: O(1). `min(h)` would be O(n)
Turn a list into a heap in place: O(n)
Push then pop, or pop then push, in one O(log n) step: for fixed-size heaps
One-off top k: about O(n log k)

sections.code:
import heapq
from itertools import count

nums = [5, 1, 8, 3, 9, 2]
heapq.heapify(nums)               # O(n), in place
print(nums[0])                    # 1  (peek)

max_heap = []                     # max-heap by negation
for x in [5, 1, 8, 3]:
    heapq.heappush(max_heap, -x)
print(-heapq.heappop(max_heap))   # 8

tie = count()                     # tie-breaker: dicts never compared
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, next(tie), {"name": "write tests"}))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, next(tie), {"name": "fix outage"}))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, next(tie), {"name": "review PR"}))
while tasks:
    priority, _, task = heapq.heappop(tasks)
    print(priority, task["name"])  # 1 fix outage, 2 write tests, 2 review PR
sections.pitfall: Pushing `-x` but forgetting to negate on the way out returns negative numbers. Write the sign convention in a comment right next to the heap, or wrap pushes and pops in two tiny helpers.

check.question: You need a max-heap of integers in Python. What do you push for the value 7?
choices: 7, then call heapq.reverse(h)
(7, True), so heapq sorts in reverse
7, and read the maximum from h[-1]
-7, and negate again when you pop
check.explanation: heapq only builds min-heaps. Negating turns the largest value into the smallest, so it rises to the root, and negating again on the way out restores it. There is no heapq.reverse, and h[-1] is just the last leaf, not the maximum.

sections.title: JavaScript has no heap: write a tiny one
sections.key: JavaScript has no heap: sort once when all the data is known, or write a short comparator-based MinHeap, and never sort numbers without a comparator.
sections.body:
JavaScript has no built-in priority queue. Name your options in an interview:

- Sort once, when all the data is known: O(n log n), often good enough.
- Re-sort after every insert: O(n log n) per operation. Avoid it inside loops.
- Write a small binary heap: about 40 lines, O(log n) per operation.

The class below takes a comparator, so one class gives several heaps:

[[visual]]

`(i - 1) >> 1` is the parent index: `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)` as a bit shift.

A classic trap: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 9]`, because the default sort compares values as strings. Always pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers.

Many interviewers accept "assume a MinHeap with push, pop and peek". Ask first, and be ready to write it.

[[code]]

visual.title: One class, several heaps
rows: Min-heap of pairs, keyed on the first element

sections.pitfall: Writing the comparator as `(a, b) => a > b`. It returns true or false instead of a negative, zero or positive number, so both this heap and `Array.prototype.sort` misbehave. Return `a - b`, or -1, 0 and 1.

activity.title: Top three with a max-heap
activity.prompt: Create a max-heap by passing a comparator, push every value from `data`, then pop three times into `top3`. The program should print `9 8 7`.

props.task: Use the MinHeap class as a max-heap so the program prints 9 8 7.

check.question: What does `[10, 9, 1, 100].sort()` return in JavaScript?
check.explanation: Without a comparator, sort converts values to strings and compares them character by character: "1" < "10" < "100" < "9". Pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numbers numerically.

sections.title: Top-k and k-way merge
sections.key: Top k: a min-heap of size k whose root, the weakest kept value, gets evicted. K-way merge: one heap entry per list. Both cost O(n log k).
sections.body:
You need the 10 highest of a million scores arriving as a stream. Sorting is O(n log n) and needs everything in memory. Instead, keep the k **largest** in a **min-heap** of size k: its root is the weakest kept value, the current kth largest.

- Fewer than k items: push.
- Otherwise, if the value beats the root, `heapreplace`; if not, ignore it.

[[visual]]

That is O(n log k) time and O(k) space, nearly linear for small k, and it works on a stream you see only once.

[[visual 2]]

Alternatives: sorting is O(n log n) and simplest to write. Quickselect finds the kth largest in O(n) average time, but O(n^2) worst case, and it rearranges the input.

visual.title: The same idea, other problems
rows: k closest points to the origin
Max-heap of size k by `x*x + y*y` (negate in Python); evict the farthest. Squares keep the order, so skip the square root
Count with a dict, then a min-heap of size k keyed by count
One `(value, list_index, element_index)` entry per list: pop, output, push that list's next. O(N log k) for N values, O(k) space
A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, sizes within one

sections.pitfall: Heapifying all n values and popping k times also works, but it costs O(n + k log n) time and O(n) space and needs all the data at once. Fine for small inputs; say why the size-k heap is better for huge inputs and streams.

activity.title: Kth largest element
activity.prompt: Solve it with a min-heap that never holds more than k values (the JavaScript starter includes a MinHeap class). Then ask yourself what changes when k is close to n.

check.question: To find the 10 largest values in a stream of a billion numbers, what do you keep while reading it?
choices: A max-heap holding every value
A min-heap holding at most 10 values
A sorted array of every value
A min-heap holding every value
check.explanation: A min-heap of size 10 keeps the best 10 so far, with the weakest at the root ready to be evicted. Anything that stores every value needs memory for a billion numbers and O(n log n) work.

sections.title: Practice: when to reach for a heap
sections.key: Reach for a heap when a problem repeatedly needs the smallest or largest item while the items keep changing; skip it for one-off minimums, full sorts or searches.
sections.body:
Heap problems hide behind a few phrases:

[[visual]]

When not to use one:

- You need the minimum once: `min()` is O(n) and simpler.
- All the data is known and you need all of it in order: just sort.
- You must search for or delete arbitrary values: finding a value in a heap is O(n). Use a hash map or a balanced tree.

In an interview, say three things out loud: min-heap or max-heap (and whether you negated values), what each entry holds, and the complexity in terms of both n and k.

visual.title: Phrases that mean heap
rows: "k largest", "kth largest", "top k", "k closest", "k most frequent"
A heap of size k: O(n log k)
"repeatedly take the two largest and combine them"
A max-heap of everything: pop two, push the result. Smashing stones works this way
"merge k sorted lists, arrays or files"
A heap keyed by time or priority
Shortest paths in a weighted graph

activity.title: Merge k sorted arrays
activity.prompt: Push one entry per array holding the value plus where it came from, then pop and refill. Watch out for empty arrays in the input.

check.question: Which task is the weakest fit for a heap?
choices: Always processing the job with the earliest deadline next
Merging 50 sorted log files into one sorted file
Keeping the 5 highest scores seen so far in a game
Checking whether a value appears anywhere in a large collection
check.explanation: A heap only knows where its root is; finding an arbitrary value means scanning the whole array, O(n). A hash set answers membership in O(1) on average. The other three are classic heap problems.

keyTerms.definition: An abstract data type where you add items and always remove the one with the highest priority.
A complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap property; the usual way to implement a priority queue.
In a min-heap every parent is less than or equal to its children (greater than or equal in a max-heap), so the root is the minimum (or maximum).
A tree whose levels are all full except possibly the last, which fills from the left, so it fits in an array with no gaps.
Swap a newly appended value with its parent while it is smaller, restoring the heap property after a push.
Swap a value at the top with its smaller child while it is larger, restoring the heap property after a pop.
Turn an unsorted array into a heap in O(n) by sifting down every non-leaf node from the last one back to the root.
Python's module of functions that treat a plain list as a min-heap: heappush, heappop, heapify, nlargest and more.
Keep a heap of size k (a min-heap for the k largest) so n items cost O(n log k) time and O(k) space.
Merge k sorted sources by keeping one entry per source in a heap, popping the smallest and refilling from the same source.

summary: A heap keeps the minimum (or maximum) at the root: peek O(1), push and pop O(log n).
Stored as an array: children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, parent at (i - 1) // 2.
Push sifts up; pop moves the last leaf to the root and sifts down past the smaller child.
heapq is a min-heap: negate for a max-heap, add a counter to break ties.
JavaScript needs a hand-written heap, and always a comparator for sort.
Top k: a min-heap of size k. K-way merge: one entry per source.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why a min-heap of size k, not a max-heap, is the right tool for finding the k largest numbers in a huge stream, and what the root of that heap tells you at every moment.

questions.question: Select every operation a binary min-heap performs in O(log n) time or better.
choices: Insert a value
Remove the minimum
Peek at the minimum
Find whether an arbitrary value is present
Return all values in sorted order
questions.explanation: Insert and remove-min each walk one root-to-leaf path, O(log n), and peeking at the root is O(1). Finding an arbitrary value requires scanning, O(n), and producing everything in sorted order means n pops, O(n log n).

questions.question: Which array is NOT a valid min-heap?
questions.explanation: In [2, 4, 3, 5, 1], the value 1 at index 4 has its parent at index (4 - 1) // 2 = 1, which holds 4. A child smaller than its parent breaks the heap property. A sorted array is always a valid min-heap, and [1, 3, 2, 7, 4] is valid because siblings are unordered.

questions.question: What is a priority queue, and how is it related to a heap?
questions.answer: A priority queue is the abstract idea: add items and always remove the one with the highest priority. A binary heap is the usual data structure that implements it, with O(log n) push and pop and O(1) peek.
questions.explanation: Keep the abstract idea (what operations you need) separate from the data structure that implements it.

questions.question: In a 0-based heap array, what index holds the left child of the node at index 4?
questions.explanation: The left child of i is 2 * i + 1 = 9, and the right child is 10.

questions.question: The min-heap array is `[2, 6, 3, 9, 7, 4]`. What are the children of the value 6?
choices: 3 and 9
9 and 7
7 and 4
4 only
questions.explanation: 6 is at index 1, so its children are at indexes 3 and 4, which hold 9 and 7. The value 3 is 6's sibling, and 4 is the child of 3 (index 5).

questions.question: Why can a heap be stored in an array with no gaps, while an arbitrary binary tree cannot?
choices: Heap values are sorted, so positions are predictable
Each heap node has exactly two children
Heaps never hold more than a few thousand nodes
A heap is a complete binary tree, filled level by level from the left
questions.explanation: Completeness means positions 0 to n - 1 are all filled, level by level, so the index formulas always land on real nodes. Heap values are not sorted, and nodes near the bottom may have one or zero children.

questions.question: A min-heap holds 100 elements. How many levels does its tree have?
questions.explanation: Full levels hold 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 nodes, 63 in total across 6 levels. The remaining 37 go on a 7th level. That matches floor(log2 100) = 6 edges of height.

questions.question: Put the steps of popping the minimum from a binary min-heap in order.
items: Save the root value to return later
Remove the last element of the array
Put that last element at the root
Swap it with its smaller child while it is larger than that child
questions.explanation: Save the root first, then fill the hole at the top with the last leaf so the tree stays complete, and sift it down to restore the heap property.

questions.question: You push 1 into the min-heap `[3, 5, 4, 8, 6]`. Write the array after sift up.
questions.explanation: 1 is appended at index 5, whose parent is index 2 (value 4): swap to get [3, 5, 1, 8, 6, 4]. Now 1 is at index 2, whose parent is index 0 (value 3): swap again to get [1, 5, 3, 8, 6, 4].

questions.question: This `sift_down` sometimes leaves an invalid min-heap. Why?
choices: The loop should start at the last index
It only looks at the left child, so a smaller right child can stay below a larger parent
It should test heap[child] > heap[i]
2 * i + 1 is the parent index, not a child index
questions.explanation: It only ever looks at the left child. If the right child is smaller than the parent (or smaller than the left child), the parent stays above a smaller value. Sift down must compare both children and swap with the smaller one.

questions.question: Why does heapify (sift down every non-leaf node, from the last one back to the root) run in O(n) rather than O(n log n)?
choices: It skips the leaves, and halving O(n log n) work gives O(n)
Sift down is O(1) when the values are random
Most nodes are near the bottom and can only sift down a few levels, so the total is O(n)
It sorts the array first with counting sort
questions.explanation: Half the nodes are leaves and do no work, a quarter can move at most one level, an eighth at most two, and so on. That series sums to O(n). Skipping the leaves alone would still leave O(n log n) if every other node could travel the full height.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time to build a heap by calling push n times on an empty heap?
choices: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Each push can sift a new value all the way up, O(log n), so n pushes cost O(n log n) in the worst case (for example, inserting values in decreasing order into a min-heap). Heapify on the whole array is O(n).

questions.question: Fill the blank to read the smallest value in O(1) without removing it.
choices: min(nums)
nums[-1]
nums[0]
heapq.heappop(nums)
questions.explanation: After heapify, the minimum is always at index 0. min(nums) gives the same value but scans the whole list, O(n), and heappop removes it. nums[-1] is just the last leaf.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import heapq

h = []
for x in [4, 1, 7, 3]:
    heapq.heappush(h, -x)
print(-heapq.heappop(h), -h[0])
questions.explanation: The heap holds -4, -1, -7 and -3, so the root is -7. Popping and negating gives 7. The new root is -4, so -h[0] is 4. The output is 7 4.

questions.question: The second push raises TypeError. Why, and what is the usual fix?
choices: heappush cannot store tuples; push the dict alone
Priorities tie, so Python compares the dicts; add a counter: (priority, count, job)
The list must be heapified before the first push
Dicts are mutable, so they cannot be stored in a list
questions.explanation: Both tuples have priority 2, so Python moves on to compare the dicts, and dicts do not support <. Adding a counter as the second element, (priority, count, job), means ties are settled by the counter and the dicts are never compared.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
import heapq

h = [5, 1, 4]        # built by hand, never heapified
print(heapq.heappop(h))
choices: It raises an error because the list is not a heap
questions.explanation: heappop assumes the list is already a heap. It removes the last element (4), returns h[0] (5), and puts 4 at the root. You get 5, not the minimum 1, and no error. Call heapq.heapify(h) first.

questions.question: Which comparator turns the JavaScript MinHeap class into a max-heap of numbers?
choices: (a, b) => b - a
(a, b) => a - b
(a, b) => a > b
(a, b) => Math.max(a, b)
questions.explanation: The class puts whatever compares as "smaller" (a negative result) at the root. (a, b) => b - a reports larger numbers as smaller, so the maximum rises to the top. a > b returns a boolean, which breaks the comparison.

questions.question: Complete the parent index in the JavaScript `push` method.
questions.explanation: (i - 1) >> 1 equals Math.floor((i - 1) / 2), the 0-based parent. i >> 1 is the 1-based formula and picks the wrong parent for even indexes (for i = 2 it gives 1 instead of 0).

questions.question: An interviewer asks for the k smallest values in JavaScript, and no heap library is available. Which response is strongest?
choices: Offer sorting first, then a small comparator-based heap for O(n log k)
Call Math.min k times, removing the result each time
Use arr.sort() without a comparator, then take the first k
Use a Set, because Sets keep their values in sorted order
questions.explanation: Mentioning the simple O(n log n) sort shows judgment, and a small comparator-based heap gets O(n log k). Calling Math.min k times is O(nk), sort without a comparator compares strings, and Sets do not keep values sorted.

questions.question: What does `[5, 25, 100, 3].sort()` return in JavaScript? Type the array.
questions.explanation: The default sort compares strings: "100" < "25" < "3" < "5", because "1" comes before "2", "3" and "5". Use (a, b) => a - b for numbers.

questions.question: To keep the k largest values from a stream, which heap do you use, and why?
choices: A max-heap of size k, because its root is the largest value
A min-heap of all values, popping k at the end
A max-heap of size k, evicting its smallest leaf
A min-heap of size k, because its root is the weakest kept value and the one to evict
questions.explanation: The kept values form the top k, and the one to throw out when a better value arrives is the smallest of them, which a min-heap keeps at the root. A max-heap of size k would have the best value at the root and no fast way to evict the worst.

questions.question: What does `kth_largest([7, 10, 4, 3, 20, 15], 3)` return?
questions.explanation: The three largest values are 20, 15 and 10. The size-3 min-heap ends up holding exactly those, and its root, 10, is the 3rd largest.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the size-k min-heap method for the kth largest of n numbers?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n log k)
O(k log n)
O(n + k)
questions.explanation: Each of the n values costs at most one O(log k) heap operation, because the heap never holds more than k items. O(n log n) is the cost of sorting everything.

questions.question: In `merge_k_sorted`, why does each heap entry store `(value, list_index, element_index)` instead of just the value?
choices: After popping a value you need to know which array it came from and where its next element is
Tuples sort faster than integers in heapq
The indexes only exist to keep equal values in a stable order
heapq cannot store plain integers
questions.explanation: After popping the smallest value you must refill the heap from the same array, which requires knowing which array it came from and where its next element is. The indexes also settle ties between equal values, but that is not their main job.

questions.question: You merge k sorted arrays holding N values in total with a heap. What are the time and the extra space, not counting the output?
choices: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
O(N k) time, O(1) space
O(N log k) time, O(k) space
O(k log N) time, O(k) space
questions.explanation: The heap never holds more than k entries, so each of the N pops and pushes costs O(log k), and the heap itself uses O(k) space. Concatenating and sorting would be O(N log N).

questions.question: This `kth_largest` gives wrong answers. What is the bug?
choices: It returns heap[-1]; the kth largest is the root, heap[0]
It should pop before pushing, not after
The heap should hold k + 1 values
heappop removes the largest value, so it evicts the wrong one
questions.explanation: The min-heap correctly ends up holding the k largest values, but heap[-1] is just the last leaf, not the kth largest. The kth largest is the smallest of the k, at the root: heap[0]. For [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4] with k = 2, it returns 6 instead of 5.

questions.question: In the k closest points problem, why compare `x*x + y*y` instead of the true distance `sqrt(x*x + y*y)`?
choices: Squaring keeps the same order for nonnegative distances, so the square root is wasted work
sqrt is not available in Python without extra packages
Squared distances turn the heap into a max-heap automatically
The true distance gives the wrong order for negative coordinates
questions.explanation: For nonnegative numbers, a < b exactly when a squared < b squared, so squared distances give the same order. Skipping the square root saves work and avoids floating point rounding.

questions.question: Match each problem with the heap setup that fits it.

pairs.right: Count, then a min-heap of size 5 keyed by count
A heap with one entry per file
A max-heap and a min-heap, balanced in size

pairs.left: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones

questions.explanation: Frequency top-k counts first, k-way merge keeps one entry per source, a running median balances two heaps, and the stone game repeatedly needs the two largest of everything.

questions.question: Which tasks are a good fit for a heap? Select all that apply.
choices: Return the 3 closest restaurants out of 50,000
Check whether a username is already taken
Always run the job with the earliest deadline next
Reverse a string
Emit events in timestamp order when they arrive slightly out of order
questions.explanation: Top-k closest, earliest deadline first and reordering events by timestamp all need "the smallest next" repeatedly. Checking whether a username exists is a hash set job, and reversing a string needs no ordering at all.

questions.question: Stones weigh `[2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 1]`. Repeatedly smash the two heaviest: equal stones both vanish, otherwise the difference remains. What weight is left at the end?
questions.explanation: 8 and 7 leave 1: [2, 4, 1, 1, 1]. 4 and 2 leave 2: [2, 1, 1, 1]. 2 and 1 leave 1: [1, 1, 1]. 1 and 1 vanish: [1]. One stone of weight 1 remains.

questions.question: You need to repeatedly delete arbitrary values (not just the minimum) and also find the minimum. Why is a plain binary heap a poor choice?
choices: Heaps cannot store duplicate values
Deleting the minimum is O(n) in a heap
Finding an arbitrary value takes O(n), because a heap is only partially ordered
Heaps only work with integers
questions.explanation: A heap is only partially ordered, so locating an arbitrary value means scanning the array, O(n). A balanced BST (or a heap plus a hash map of positions, or lazy deletion) handles this better. Deleting the minimum itself is O(log n), and heaps handle duplicates and any comparable values.
